case_title: Deepak Sakharam Kulkarni & Connected Matters vs. Manoj Kumar Agarwal, RP of D.S. Kulkarni Developers Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 63 of 2024 with Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 1142, 1307, 1308, 1223, 1226, 1660, 1050, 1051, 1361, 1385 of 2023
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (Chairperson Ashok Bhushan and Technical Member Barun Mitra)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants include Promoters (Deepak & Shirish Kulkarni), Group Entities (DS Kulkarni & Co., DSK Global Education), Homebuyers (allottees of Anandghan and Madhukosh projects), and Operational Creditors/Employees. Respondent No. 1 is Manoj Kumar Agarwal, RP of D.S. Kulkarni Developers Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). Respondents Nos. 2-4 comprise the Consortium SRA (Ashdan Properties, Classic Promoters, and Atul Builders). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was a major real estate company undergoing CIRP initiated by Bank of Maharashtra under Section 7 on 26.09.2019. CIRP yielded a resolution plan approved by the CoC on 13.08.2021 with an 83.37% vote share. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose on bank credit facilities exceeding statutory thresholds; SRA's approved resolution plan provided an outlay of Rs. 826.30 Crores (with Rs. 30 Crores upfront and deferred balance) against claims exceeding Rs. 1,900 Crores. Payout to operational creditors was 0.368% and employees 0.97%. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 26.09.2019. NCLT excluded time via orders dated 11.01.2022 and 20.06.2022 extending CIRP to cover the CoC plan approval on 13.08.2021. RP filed approval IA No. 1950/2021 on 24.08.2021. NCLT Mumbai approved the plan on 23.06.2023, subsequently dismissing homebuyers' pending claim IAs as infructuous on 01.08.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered sale deeds dated 07.06.2002 for 41R land at Bavdhan; 99-year Lease Deed dated 24.09.2008 in favor of DSK Global; registered tripartite agreements dated 30.06.2017; allotment letters dated April 2017; bank ledgers; MahaRERA order dated 05.02.2018; and registered valuation reports. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I approved the resolution plan on 23.06.2023 in IA No. 1950/2021 and rejected homebuyer claim applications on 01.08.2023. Eleven connected appeals were filed before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: (i) Whether a resolution plan can validly extinguish third-party property rights by confiscating land owned by a partnership firm or cancelling a 99-year lease and appropriating college buildings without statutory termination and compensation under Section 18(1)(f) and Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC; (ii) Whether the RP and SRA can reject homebuyer claims supported by genuine pre-CIRP allotment letters and registered tripartite agreements on the ground that payments were credited to group entities rather than the corporate debtor's bank accounts; (iii) Whether approved resolution plans can be challenged on low valuation or meagre payouts to operational creditors (0.368%) and employees (0.97%) absent violation of Section 30(2)(b).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 18(1)(f) and its Explanation, the asset pool of a corporate debtor in CIRP cannot include assets owned by third parties or subsidiaries; a resolution plan cannot be utilized as a device to expropriate third-party land or unilaterally extinguish long-term leasehold and building rights without adhering to due process of law under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, as such clauses violate Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC. Furthermore, genuine pre-CIRP allotment letters acknowledging payment bind the corporate debtor and qualify purchasers as allottees under Section 5(8)(f). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18(1)(f) Explanation expressly excludes third-party assets held under contractual arrangements. An un-terminated 99-year lease cannot be extinguished by resolution plan fiat without paying contractual building construction costs. Under Section 5(8)(f), consideration acknowledged by the corporate debtor for apartment allotments constitutes an amount raised under a real estate transaction having the commercial effect of borrowing. Regarding operational payouts, commercial wisdom of the CoC governs distribution under Section 30(2)(b) unless the liquidation threshold is breached. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified registered 2002 sale deeds establishing separate title over 41R Bavdhan land, registered 99-year lease covenants requiring construction compensation, bank ledgers verifying payments for homebuyer apartments, and valuation compliance under Regulations 27 and 35. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Offending clauses expropriating DSK Global's building and DSK & Co.'s 41R land were severed and deleted; homebuyer claims were directed to be admitted and provided units under the plan; operational and promoter challenges were dismissed.
operative_order: Company Appeal Nos. 63/2024, 1142/2023, 1223/2023, and 1226/2023 are dismissed. Appeal No. 1307/2023 is partly allowed, modifying Appendix-IV Item No. 10 to exclude 0H41R land of DSK & Co.. Appeal No. 1308/2023 is partly allowed, deleting Clauses 13.4, 13.5, and 13.6 of the plan to preserve DSK Global's lease/building rights. Appeal Nos. 1361, 1385, 1660, 1050, and 1051 of 2023 are allowed, directing the RP and SRA to admit the appellants as homebuyers and allot them units as per the plan. The NCLT approval order dated 23.06.2023 is upheld as modified. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: Multiple stakeholders appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order approving the resolution plan for D.S. Kulkarni Developers Ltd. submitted by a consortium led by Ashdan Properties. Appellants included promoters alleging undervaluation, group entities challenging expropriation of their separate land and 99-year leasehold college buildings, homebuyers whose claims were rejected due to payments routed via group firms, and operational creditors receiving 0.368%. Partly allowing the appeals, the NCLAT Principal Bench severed and deleted plan clauses unlawfully extinguishing third-party lease and land titles under Section 18(1)(f) and Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC. The Tribunal ordered the admission of all bona fide homebuyers who held pre-CIRP allotment letters and directed the SRA to provide them units under the plan.

case_title: Paras Builders and Promoters vs. ASREC India Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1016 of 2024 & I.A. No. 3696 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Paras Builders and Promoters, Promoters through executive partners (Appellant); ASREC India Ltd. & Ors. (Respondents); Bank of India (Original Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 7 application filed by Bank of India against the corporate debtor, where ASREC India was substituted as financial creditor via an assignment agreement dated March 30, 2022. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on credit facilities extended to the corporate debtor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Assignment agreement executed on March 30, 2022; Section 7 application admitted on March 31, 2023; NCLT rejected recall application (IA 380/2023) on February 2, 2024; appeal filed with 9 days' condoned delay. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Assignment agreement substituting ASREC, pending civil suits challenging the assignment and SARFAESI measures. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT rejected the promoters' application (IA 380/2023) seeking recall of the Section 7 admission order, prompting the promoters' appeal.
legal_issues: Whether an order admitting a Section 7 application can be recalled on the ground that the underlying assignment agreement is challenged in civil proceedings or that SARFAESI measures are sub-judice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Pending civil suits challenging an assignment agreement or ongoing SARFAESI proceedings do not constitute valid grounds to stay or recall a Section 7 insolvency admission order. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The grounds for recalling an admission order are strictly circumscribed by the 5-member bench judgment in Union Bank of India v. Dinkar T. Venkatasubramanian, and external civil disputes do not fall within those permissible grounds. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The existence of an undisputed debt and default justifies Section 7 admission regardless of collateral civil challenges to debt assignments. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Adjudicating Authority found valid debt and default and the recall application fell outside permissible review grounds, the appeal lacks merit.
operative_order: I.A. No. 3696 of 2024 (delay condonation) is allowed, and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1016 of 2024 is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: Paras Builders and Promoters, represented by its executive partners, appealed against an NCLT order dated February 2, 2024 rejecting their application (IA 380/2023) to recall a Section 7 admission order[cite: 62]. The appellants argued that the assignment agreement favoring ASREC was challenged in a civil court and SARFAESI proceedings were pending[cite: 62]. NCLAT held, following the 5-member bench ruling in Union Bank of India v. Dinkar T. Venkatasubramanian, that collateral civil disputes cannot form the basis for recalling a Section 7 admission order[cite: 62]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 62].

case_title: O.A.A. Ananthapadmanaban Chettiar vs. Sri Mahalakshmi Textiles
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is O.A.A. Ananthapadmanaban Chettiar, shareholder of Corporate Debtor M/s. Annamalaiar Textiles Private Limited (MILLS); Respondent is M/s. Sri Mahalakshmi Textiles (Converter/Financial Creditor)[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Memorandum of Understanding and Agreement for Conversion dated 03.08.2006, whereby Respondent agreed to advance Rs. 45 Lakhs interest-free and incur machinery overhauling/startup expenses to make the Corporate Debtor operational as a start-up from 09.08.2006, in exchange for delivery of converted cotton yarn counts at agreed conversion rates[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from failure to repay the advanced sums and overhauling expenses upon expiry of the conversion agreement; default amount not specified in the order[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreements executed on 03.08.2006; letter for appointment of arbitrator issued on 05.02.2008; Section 7 petition admitted by NCLT Single Bench Chennai on 07.08.2018[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MoU dated 03.08.2006 stipulating that all expenses incurred towards machinery overhauling, electrification, and start-up works shall be treated as an interest-free loan to the mills, repayable upon expiry or deducted through yarn supply[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Single Bench admitted Respondent's Section 7 petition on 07.08.2018, declared a moratorium, and appointed an IRP; Appellant shareholder appealed contending Respondent was not a financial creditor and the claim was barred by limitation[cite: 29].
legal_issues: Whether an advance extended under a conversion agreement to overhaul machinery and operationalize a manufacturing mill in exchange for commercial finished goods output constitutes a financial debt disbursed for the time value of money under Section 5(8) of the IBC; and whether the petition was barred by limitation[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Commercial advances and expenditure incurred to rehabilitate and startup a manufacturing unit, repayable in the form of subsidized conversion rates and delivery of manufactured inventory, constitute disbursements against consideration for the time value of money, qualifying the transaction as a financial debt under Section 5(8)[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) does not mandate purely monetary interest returns; commercial returns in the form of product delivery (yarn conversion) satisfy the time value of money requirement. Under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, limitation began upon enactment of the Code, making the Section 7 petition timely[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of contractual covenants in the conversion agreement demonstrating disbursement of funds structured as an interest-free loan with defined economic return mechanisms[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The converter was a Financial Creditor owed a valid financial debt in default, and arbitration notices did not bar a Section 7 petition[cite: 29].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the impugned admission order dated 7th August, 2018 passed by NCLT Single Bench Chennai is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 29].
summary: Appellant O.A.A. Ananthapadmanaban Chettiar, shareholder of Annamalaiar Textiles Pvt. Ltd., appealed against NCLT Chennai's order dated 7 August 2018 admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by Sri Mahalakshmi Textiles[cite: 29]. Appellant contended that an interest-free startup advance granted under a 2006 conversion agreement was not a financial debt under Section 5(8) and was time-barred[cite: 29]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that funds disbursed to overhaul plant machinery in exchange for manufactured yarn delivery satisfy the time value of money test under Section 5(8), and that pending arbitration is no defense to an admitted financial default under Section 7[cite: 29].

case_title: Citi Securities & Financial Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. Sudip Bhattacharya, Resolution Professional of Reliance Naval & Engineering Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Reliance Naval & Engineering Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Reliance Infrastructure Limited is the original lender and a related party; Citi Securities & Financial Services Pvt. Ltd. is the Assignee/Appellant claiming status as Financial Creditor; Sudip Bhattacharya is Respondent No. 1 (Resolution Professional); Committee of Creditors represented via IDBI Bank Ltd. is Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Reliance Infrastructure Limited extended Rs. 2,500 Crores as interest-bearing Inter-Corporate Deposits (ICDs) to the Corporate Debtor, secured via Deed of Hypothecation and Indenture of Mortgage dated 07.03.2018. On 01.03.2019, Reliance Infrastructure Limited assigned the debt of Rs. 2,284,88,96,502 together with all rights, securities, and liabilities to the Appellant for a consideration of Rs. 114.93 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was declared an NPA by IDBI Bank on 28.02.2018. Appellant submitted a Form C claim of Rs. 25,38,20,01,492/- to the IRP on 29.01.2020 based on the 01.03.2019 assignment. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed by IDBI Bank in September 2018; Assignment Deed executed on 01.03.2019 during the pendency of the Section 7 petition; Section 7 petition admitted on 15.01.2020; Appellant filed claim on 29.01.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Assignment Deed dated 01.03.2019 transferring debt with underlying mortgages/hypothecation; lack of bank transaction entries proving actual payment of Rs. 114.93 Crores consideration; failure to register the Assignment Deed or pay requisite stamp duty under the Maharashtra Stamp Act; SEBI Show Cause Notice dated 11.02.2022 highlighting circular transactions between Reliance group entities and Appellant. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor was admitted to CIRP on 15.01.2020 in CP (IB) 418/AHD/2018. Resolution Professional declined to admit Appellant's claim as Financial Creditor. Appellant filed IA No. 02 of 2021 before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court No. 2, which dismissed the application on 22.02.2022 holding the Appellant disqualified as a related party under the first proviso to Section 21(2) IBC and rejecting the unstamped/unregistered Assignment Deed.
legal_issues: 1. Whether an Assignment Deed transferring a debt along with underlying mortgage and hypothecation security constitutes an actionable claim or an instrument requiring compulsory registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908 and adequate stamp duty under the Maharashtra Stamp Act. 2. Whether an assignee acquiring debt from a related party during the pendency of Section 7 proceedings for nominal consideration is disqualified from the Committee of Creditors and admission of claim under the first proviso to Section 21(2) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An assignment transferring a debt secured by mortgage of immovable property and hypothecation of movable property is excluded from the definition of an actionable claim and requires compulsory registration and requisite stamping to be admissible in evidence. Furthermore, where a related-party creditor assigns debt to an ostensible third party as a commercial contrivance to circumvent the statutory bar under the first proviso to Section 21(2) of the IBC and gain backdoor entry into the CoC, the assignee remains disqualified. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Actionable claim under Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act explicitly excludes debts secured by mortgage of immovable property or hypothecation; hence Section 17(1)(b) and (c) read with Section 49 of the Registration Act renders unregistered assignments inadmissible. Section 21(2) first proviso, construed purposively in light of Phoenix ARC, debars assignees who acquire debts through bad-faith contrivances to sabotage CIRP or dilute voting shares. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal evaluates the bona fides of the assignment. Transfer of a Rs. 2,538 Crore secured debt for a meager Rs. 114.93 Crores during pending Section 7 proceedings without bank ledger verification demonstrates an un-bona fide contrivance. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Assignment Deed was legally inadmissible for want of registration and stamp duty, and the assignment was a device to bypass related-party disqualification; thus, rejection of the claim was valid.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 240 of 2022 is dismissed. The order dated 22.02.2022 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court No. 2) rejecting IA No. 02 of 2021 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Citi Securities & Financial Services Pvt. Ltd. challenged NCLT Ahmedabad Bench's order rejecting its application to be admitted as a Financial Creditor of Corporate Debtor Reliance Naval & Engineering Limited for Rs. 2,538 Crores. Appellant claimed debt via an assignment from Reliance Infrastructure Limited, a related party, during pending Section 7 proceedings. NCLAT held that the assignment deed transferred underlying mortgage and hypothecation rights, failing the definition of actionable claim and requiring mandatory registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908 and adequate stamping under the Maharashtra Stamp Act. Furthermore, the assignment for a nominal sum was an un-bona fide contrivance for backdoor entry into the CoC, violating Section 21(2) IBC. Consequently, NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Pramod Kumar Pathak vs. Arfat Petrochemicals Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pramod Kumar Pathak is Appellant (representative of workmen union of M/s J.K. Synthetics Pvt. Ltd.); Arfat Petrochemicals Private Limited is Respondent (Corporate Debtor / scheme implementer). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: J.K. Synthetics Pvt. Ltd. was declared a sick industrial unit by BIFR on 02.04.1998. An MoU was executed with Respondent, based upon which AAIFR approved and sanctioned a rehabilitation scheme on 07.01.2005 under SICA, 1985. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant alleged continuing contravention of the sanctioned rehabilitation scheme dated 07.01.2005 and failure to meet liabilities toward workmen, while Respondent contended dues had been inspected and settled under a High Court-appointed retired judge, with Appellant's claim being under Rs. 1 Lakh. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: AAIFR sanctioned scheme 07.01.2005; Central Government Notification S.O. 1683(E) issued 24.05.2017; Appellant filed CP(IB) 395 of 2020 under Section 33 read with Section 34 IBC before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: AAIFR sanctioned rehabilitation scheme dated 07.01.2005; Central Government Removal of Difficulties Order dated 24.05.2017; inspection report of Justice N.N. Mathur (Retd.); Supreme Court judgment in Spartek Ceramics India Ltd. dated 25.10.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an application under Section 33 read with Section 34 IBC seeking liquidation of the Corporate Debtor for contravention of the 2005 SICA rehabilitation scheme. On 22.12.2021, NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-1 dismissed the application, holding that the 2005 scheme was not a resolution plan under Section 5(26) IBC and Section 33 was inapplicable. Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: 1. Whether a rehabilitation scheme sanctioned under Section 18 of SICA, 1985 can be deemed an approved resolution plan under Section 31(1) and Section 5(26) of the IBC pursuant to Central Government Notification S.O. 1683(E) dated 24.05.2017. 2. Whether an application for liquidation under Section 33(4) of the IBC is maintainable for the alleged contravention of a SICA rehabilitation scheme.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A rehabilitation scheme sanctioned under the repealed Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 cannot be deemed an approved resolution plan under Section 31(1) of the IBC. An application under Section 33(4) of the IBC seeking liquidation for alleged contravention of a pre-IBC SICA scheme is incompetent and non-maintainable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242 of the IBC authorizes the Central Government to issue orders solely to remove difficulties arising in giving effect to the provisions of the IBC itself. Notification S.O. 1683(E) dated 24.05.2017, which sought to address difficulties arising from the repeal of SICA and omission of Companies Act provisions, travels beyond the statutory remit of Section 242 and is invalid, as confirmed by the Supreme Court in Spartek Ceramics. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Liquidation under Section 33(4) requires strict proof of contravention of a resolution plan approved by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31 of the IBC. A sanctioned SICA scheme cannot meet this threshold. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Notification dated 24.05.2017 having been ruled ultra vires, the 2005 scheme cannot be treated as a resolution plan under Section 5(26) IBC, rendering Section 33 liquidation proceedings unmaintainable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 312 of 2022 is dismissed. The impugned order dated 22.12.2021 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-1 in CP(IB) 395 of 2020 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Pramod Kumar Pathak, representing workmen of J.K. Synthetics Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench's dismissal of an application filed under Section 33 read with Section 34 of the IBC seeking liquidation of Arfat Petrochemicals Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant alleged breach of an AAIFR rehabilitation scheme sanctioned in 2005, arguing that the Central Government's Removal of Difficulties Order dated 24.05.2017 deemed SICA schemes as approved resolution plans under Section 31 IBC. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that pursuant to the Supreme Court's ruling in Spartek Ceramics, the 2017 Notification traveled beyond Section 242 IBC and was invalid. Consequently, the SICA scheme was not a resolution plan, rendering liquidation proceedings under Section 33 unmaintainable.

case_title: Muhamad Yavar Dhala vs. Kavita Surana, Liquidator of Forward Shoes (India) Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Muhamad Yavar Dhala is the Promoter/Ex-Director of Forward Shoes (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor in Liquidation); Respondent is Kavita Surana (Liquidator). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Settlement/compromise schemes proposed under Section 230 of Companies Act involving joint development of the corporate debtor's land assets with real estate developers (Sri Ram Properties and Vijay Raja Homes Pvt. Ltd.) to generate approx. Rs. 150 crores for creditor payouts. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dues of secured and operational creditors against liquidation property estimated at Rs. 60–67 crores, with settlement schemes targeting debt resolution of Rs. 150 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation order passed on 11.12.2018; Section 230 compromise schemes submitted on 25.09.2019; MSME registration applied for on 27.12.2019 and certificate dated 02.04.2018 produced; NCLT Chennai rejected schemes via orders in MA/1322/2019 and MA/1323/2019 on 31.01.2020; asset auction conducted on 25.09.2020; LOI issued to bidder on 27.11.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Proposed schemes under Section 230 naming Appellant as sole 'Applicant' with exclusive authority and power of attorney; MSME Certificate obtained during CIRP/Liquidation showing plant and machinery investment of only Rs. 2 lakhs against assets worth Rs. 67 crores; Liquidator's status reports. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor was ordered into liquidation on 11.12.2018; Appellant submitted compromise schemes; Liquidator sought directions under Section 230; NCLT Chennai Division Bench-I dismissed the schemes on 31.01.2020 holding Appellant ineligible under Section 29A and finding the MSME certificate fraudulent.
legal_issues: Whether a promoter disqualified under Section 29A of the IBC can propose a compromise or arrangement scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act during liquidation; and whether an ex-promoter can obtain an MSME certificate post-liquidation without the liquidator to claim Section 240A exemption.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A promoter ineligible under Section 29A of the IBC is disqualified from submitting a scheme of compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 during liquidation; an ex-promoter cannot unilaterally bypass the liquidator to procure an MSME certificate after insolvency commencement to circumvent Section 29A. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 35 vests exclusive management and liquidation duties in the liquidator, while Section 33(7) operates as a discharge of corporate officers; hence, former management possesses no legal standing to independently apply for statutory certifications or manage affairs. Section 240A exemptions cannot be secured post-facto through unauthorized MSME filings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of scheme terms revealing that the promoter retains de facto operational control and powers of attorney disproves the contention of acting merely as a benign 'facilitator'. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The schemes were an unlawful attempt at back-door entry by a Section 29A disqualified promoter, rendering NCLT's refusal to sanction meetings under Section 230 unassailable.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed. Orders of NCLT Chennai in MA/1322/2019 and MA/1323/2019 rejecting the schemes upheld. No orders as to costs.
summary: Promoter of Forward Shoes (India) Pvt. Ltd. (in liquidation) appealed against an NCLT Chennai order rejecting compromise schemes submitted under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 in partnership with real estate developers. Appellant claimed exemption from Section 29A ineligibility via an MSME certificate under Section 240A. The NCLAT held that Section 29A disqualifications apply to Section 230 schemes during liquidation. Because powers and custody of the debtor vest entirely in the Liquidator under Section 35 and Section 33(7), an ex-promoter cannot unilaterally obtain an MSME registration post-CIRP to bypass statutory bars. The schemes were held to be impermissible back-door attempts to regain corporate assets.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Krishidhan Seeds Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Financial Creditor/Appellant) vs. Krishidhan Seeds Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities sanctioned by State Bank of India to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt repayment declared and classified as NPA; date of default expressly recorded as 10.06.2014 in the Section 7 petition. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Date of default: 10.06.2014; recovery proceedings before DRT instituted on 20.10.2015; OTS proposals dated 13.06.2015 and 06.11.2015; Section 7 petition filed before NCLT on 19.09.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unilateral OTS proposal letters dated 13.06.2015 and 06.11.2015 whereby Corporate Debtor proposed raising investor funds to settle lender liabilities, relied upon by the bank as an acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act; DRT application records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application filed before NCLT Indore Bench at Ahmedabad Court-1; dismissed on 16.09.2020 as barred by limitation under Article 137.
legal_issues: Whether an acknowledgment of liability in an OTS proposal can extend the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act for filing a Section 7 application under the IBC beyond three years from the date of default.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The period of limitation for a Section 7 petition under Article 137 of the Limitation Act is three years reckoned strictly from the date of default, and an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 cannot shift or extend the date of default for triggering CIRP. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238A applies the Limitation Act to IBC proceedings; however, the limitation period of three years under Article 137 runs from the actual date of default and is extendable only via Section 5 (condonation of delay), not through Section 18 acknowledgment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: There cannot be two separate dates of default for the same debt (one for DRT proceedings and one for the IBC); the date of default specified in Form 1 is absolute and determinative. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the petition was filed on 19.09.2018 for a default occurring on 10.06.2014, it was barred by limitation, and Section 18 was unavailable to salvage the application.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed in limine without costs, upholding the NCLT Indore Bench order dated 16.09.2020.
summary: State Bank of India appealed the rejection of its Section 7 petition against Krishidhan Seeds Pvt. Ltd. by NCLT Indore Bench on limitation grounds. The bank argued that the Corporate Debtor's OTS proposals dated 13.06.2015 and 06.11.2015 constituted written acknowledgments under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, extending the 3-year limitation period from the original default date of 10.06.2014 to make the 19.09.2018 filing timely. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal in limine, ruling that limitation under Article 137 runs inexorably from the default date and cannot be extended by Section 18 acknowledgment (a decision later overturned by the Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 910 of 2021).

case_title: Anup Sushil Dubey vs. National Agriculture Co-operative Marketing Federation of India Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Anup Sushil Dubey is suspended Board Member of Corporate Debtor Umarai Worldwide (P) Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is NAFED (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Krishna Gopal Ratnlal Maheshwari (IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Leave and Licence Agreement dated 01.10.2015 for 3 years for cold storage facilities at license fee of Rs. 9,31,000/- per month (with 10% annual escalation) plus 21% interest on delayed payments. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in monthly rentals, electricity, and water charges from September 2017 onwards amounting to Rs. 2,14,14,560/- (demanded Rs. 1,83,45,278/- in Form 3). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Eviction notice issued 24.05.2018; Section 8 Demand Notice issued on 26.09.2018; reply sent on 10.11.2018 (beyond statutory 10 days); Section 9 petition filed in 2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Invoices, debit notes, ledger accounts showing service tax, debt acknowledgment letters dated 01.06.2017 and 26.02.2018, and Corporate Debtor's letter dated 19.09.2018 admitting arrears, offering Rs. 11,06,028/- payment, and seeking a 2-year license renewal. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench in CP IB-522/MB/2019 admitted Section 9 CIRP on 20.12.2019 after Corporate Debtor failed to appear.
legal_issues: Whether lease/licence fees arising out of the grant of commercial leave and licence of immovable property constitute an 'Operational Debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC, and whether subsequent disputes raised in an untimely reply bar Section 9 admission.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Dues arising from the lease or license of premises for commercial purposes constitute a claim in respect of the provision of services and qualify as an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: 'Operational debt' under Section 5(21) includes commercial leasing services, supported by the BLRC Report, CGST Act (Schedule II classifying commercial leasing as a service), and the Supreme Court's pronouncements in Mobilox. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To establish a pre-existing dispute under Section 8(2) and Section 9(5)(2)(d), the dispute must be real, plausible, and supported by contemporaneous evidence prior to demand notice; assertions contradicted by written requests for lease extensions are spurious. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Commercial cold storage licence dues are operational debts; Corporate Debtor's letter of 19.09.2018 proved subsistence of debt and absence of dispute; Section 9 admission upheld.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 229 of 2020 is dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT Mumbai admission order dated 20.12.2019.
summary: NAFED entered into a 3-year commercial leave and licence agreement with Umarai Worldwide (P) Ltd. for cold storage facilities. Corporate Debtor defaulted on licence fees from September 2017. Following an unheeded Section 8 notice, NCLT Mumbai admitted NAFED's Section 9 application. The suspended director appealed, arguing that lease rent is not an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) and asserting pre-existing disputes. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that letting premises for commercial operations constitutes a service falling under Section 5(21) operational debt, and finding that letters seeking lease extensions conclusively disproved any pre-existing dispute.
